t: Minimum Changes to Make K Semi-palindromes
o: Partition s into exactly k contiguous substrings minimizing total letter changes so each piece is a semi-palindrome (some proper divisor d of its length makes all d residue classes palindromic). With n ≤ 200 we can afford to precompute the change-cost of every substring, then run a partition DP over lengths and piece counts.
k: Cost of a substring depends only on the substring: for each divisor d, count mismatched symmetric pairs inside each residue class; take the minimum over d.
Once cost[i][j] is known, standard interval-partition DP gives the answer: dp[c][j] = min over split points of dp[c-1][i] + cost(i, j).
Length-1 substrings need no divisor check (they're trivially semi-palindromes with 0 changes).

a.i: For every substring s[i..j], enumerate divisors d of its length L (d < L). Within residue class r, pair position t with mirrored position m−1−t (m = L/d characters per class); each mismatch costs one change. Take the cheapest d. Then dp over prefixes: dp[c][j] is the min cost splitting the first j characters into c pieces.
s: Build cost[i][j] for all 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n by trying each divisor d of L = j−i+1 and counting mismatches per residue class.
Transition dp[c][j] = min over i < j of dp[c-1][i] + cost[i][j-1].
a.t: O(n³ · d(n)) roughly — cost table enumerates divisors per substring, DP adds O(k·n²)
a.sp: O(n²) — cost table and DP table

w: The key realization is decoupling: substring cost is independent of the partition, so precompute it once. Pitfalls: length-1 pieces cost 0 (no valid divisor), and d ranges only over proper divisors. Follow-up: compute costs faster using the fact that mismatch counts for divisor d can be aggregated from smaller periods.
